_comment: Panic knowledge base. You can edit this file to add your own codes. Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions. 'models' entries are ProductType prefixes (e.g. 'iPhone12,' = iPhone 11 / 11 Pro / 11 Pro Max / SE 2). Restart the app after editing.

PRS0.name: Barometer (pressure sensor)
PRS0.location: Charging port flex (on iPhone 8 / X and newer the barometer sits on the charging port flex cable)

locations.location: Main logic board area near the charging port (iPhone 7 / 7 Plus). Check the charging port flex and its connector first.

steps: Fit a known-good, good-quality charging port flex (original or high-quality copy). Cheap flexes often have no barometer or a bad one, which causes this exact panic.
If the panic continues: inspect the charging flex connector on the board for corrosion, liquid damage, bent or missing pins. Clean with IPA and reseat.

Measure the charging flex connector pins in diode mode and compare with a known-good board or the schematic values. An OL (open) reading on the barometer data or power lines means a broken trace or pad.
On stacked boards (iPhone X and newer) an open line can be in the interposer. Separate the board and check the interposer pads for that line, then repair (jumper or reball).

MIC1.name: Microphone 1 (bottom microphone)
MIC1.location: Charging port flex (bottom microphone sits on the charging flex on iPhone 11 and newer)
steps: Fit a known-good charging port flex.
If the panic continues: inspect and clean the charging flex connector on the board.
Measure the charging flex connector pins in diode mode against a known-good board. Look for open (OL) mic data or power lines.
On stacked boards check the interposer for the mic lines, then the audio codec circuit.

MIC2.name: Microphone 2 (secondary microphone)
MIC2.location: A top or side flex. Depending on the model this is the power/flash flex, the earpiece/front sensor flex or the rear camera area. Confirm with the schematic for this model.
steps: Find which flex carries mic2 for this model (schematic or board viewer).
Fit a known-good copy of that flex.
If the panic continues: clean and diode-test that flex connector on the board against a known-good board.
Repair any open line (trace, pad, interposer).

MIC3.name: Microphone 3
MIC3.location: A top or rear flex depending on the model. Confirm with the schematic for this model.
steps: Find which flex carries mic3 for this model and fit a known-good copy.
Clean and diode-test that flex connector on the board.

TG0B.name: Battery temperature sensor (NTC in the battery)
steps: Fit a known-good battery (a non-genuine or damaged battery is the most common cause).
If the panic continues: inspect the battery connector on the board for damage or corrosion and clean it.
Diode-test the battery connector pins (especially the NTC / BATT_SWI lines) against a known-good board.
Repair any open line or replace the damaged connector.

TG0V.name: Battery sensor (gas gauge temperature/voltage reading)
steps: Fit a known-good battery.
Inspect and clean the battery connector on the board.
Diode-test the battery connector pins against a known-good board and repair any open line.

TG0H.name: Battery-related temperature sensor
steps: Fit a known-good battery.
Inspect, clean and diode-test the battery connector.

unknown_sensor.name: Unlisted sensor
unknown_sensor.location: Unknown. Look up this sensor code in the schematic or board viewer for this model.
steps: Find which part or flex carries this sensor in the schematic or board viewer.
Fit a known-good copy of that part or flex.
Clean and diode-test its connector and lines against a known-good board.

thermalmonitord.why: The thermal monitor service stopped checking in. iOS reboots the phone when it cannot read all of its temperature sensors. This is almost always a missing sensor on a flex (charging flex, battery, top flex) rather than a software fault.
steps: Look at the 'Missing sensor(s)' line in this log (if present) and follow the steps for that sensor.
If no sensor is listed: try a known-good charging port flex and battery first, these carry most of the sensors.
Disconnect flexes one by one (front sensor flex, power flex, camera) and watch whether the 3-minute reboot changes.
If all flexes are good, update or restore iOS to rule out software.

wifid.why: The Wi-Fi service stopped responding, which usually means iOS cannot talk to the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chip.
steps: Check whether Wi-Fi is greyed out in Settings.
Restore iOS to rule out software.
Inspect the Wi-Fi chip area for liquid damage or impact.
Measure the Wi-Fi chip power rails and reflow/replace the Wi-Fi module if needed.

backboardd.why: backboardd handles the screen and touch. A hang here points to the display, touch, or front sensor path.
steps: Try a known-good screen.
Disconnect the front camera / sensor flex and test again.
Clean and diode-test the display and touch connectors on the board.

mediaserverd.why: The media service stopped responding, which often points at the audio path (audio codec, amplifiers, speaker or mic flex).
steps: Disconnect the loudspeaker and earpiece and test again.
Try a known-good charging flex (carries a mic).
Check the audio codec and amplifier circuits on the board.

audiomxd.why: The audio service stopped responding, which often points at the audio path (audio codec, amplifiers, speaker or mic flex).
steps: Disconnect the loudspeaker and earpiece and test again.
Try a known-good charging flex (carries a mic).
Check the audio codec and amplifier circuits on the board.

CommCenter.why: CommCenter talks to the cellular modem. A hang here usually means the baseband is not responding.
steps: Check whether the phone shows 'No Service' or no IMEI.
Restore iOS to rule out software.
Check the baseband CPU, baseband PMU and their power rails (stacked boards: check the interposer).

locationd.why: The location service stopped responding. This can come from motion sensors, GPS, or the baseband.
steps: Restore iOS to rule out software.
Check the baseband and sensor circuits.

bluetoothd.why: The Bluetooth service stopped responding, which usually means iOS cannot reach the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chip.
steps: Restore iOS to rule out software.
Check the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chip and its power rails.

SpringBoard.why: SpringBoard is the home screen app. A hang here is most often software, not hardware.
steps: Update iOS, or back up and restore the phone with iTunes / 3uTools.
If the panic returns on a clean restore, look for other hardware clues in later panic logs.

rules.title: I2C bus stuck
rules.why: The log says I2C bus {g1} is stuck: a chip on that bus is holding the data (SDA) or clock (SCL) line low. This happens when a part on that bus is shorted, failed or disconnected, or when the line's pull-up resistor is damaged.
steps: Look up which chips and flexes are on I2C bus {g1} for this model in the schematic / board viewer.
Disconnect the flexes on that bus one by one (charging flex, front flex, camera) and test after each.
Measure the SDA/SCL lines of bus {g1}: voltage should be about 1.8 V and diode readings should match a known-good board. A line pulled to 0 V points to the chip holding it low.
Remove or replace the suspect chip; also check the pull-up resistors on that bus.

rules.title: Baseband (cellular modem) problem
rules.why: The panic mentions the baseband. iOS reboots when it cannot talk to the cellular modem.
steps: Check for 'No Service', no IMEI or no modem firmware in Settings > General > About.
Restore iOS to rule out a software problem.
Check the baseband CPU and baseband PMU power rails; on stacked boards check the interposer.
Reball or replace the baseband CPU if the rails are good.

rules.title: Wi-Fi / Bluetooth chip problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth driver. iOS could not get a response from the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chip.
steps: Check whether Wi-Fi is greyed out in Settings.
Restore iOS to rule out software.
Check the Wi-Fi chip power rails and the chip area for liquid or impact damage.
Reflow or replace the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth module.

rules.title: Storage (NAND) problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the storage controller (ANS / NVMe). iOS could not read or write the NAND storage correctly.
steps: Back up the data if the phone still boots.
Restore iOS with iTunes / 3uTools. Errors during restore (for example 4013, 4014, 9) also point to the NAND.
Check the NAND power rails and the NAND / CPU solder joints.
Reball or replace the NAND (needs NAND programming / SysCFG on older models).

rules.title: Secure Enclave (SEP) panic
rules.why: The Secure Enclave crashed. This can be caused by a faulty Touch ID / Face ID part, NAND problems, or the CPU itself.
steps: Disconnect Touch ID / Face ID parts and test.
Restore iOS.
If it continues, suspect the NAND or CPU (board-level).

rules.title: Touch ID problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the Touch ID (Mesa) driver.
steps: Disconnect the Touch ID / home button flex and test again.
Try a known-good home button flex (note: only the original button supports Touch ID).
Check the Touch ID connector and its lines on the board.

rules.title: Face ID problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the Face ID (Pearl) driver.
steps: Disconnect the Face ID dot projector / flood illuminator and front sensor flex and test again.
Inspect the Face ID connector for liquid damage.
Check the Face ID lines on the board.

rules.title: Camera problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the camera / image processor driver.
steps: Disconnect the rear and front cameras one at a time and test.
Fit known-good cameras.
Inspect and diode-test the camera connectors on the board.

rules.title: Display problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the display controller (DCP / CLCD).
steps: Try a known-good screen.
Inspect and clean the display connector.
Check the display power and data lines on the board.

rules.title: Touch screen problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the touch driver.
steps: Try a known-good screen.
Check the touch connector and the touch IC circuit on the board.

rules.title: Power management (PMU / SPMI) problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the power management chip or its bus. Often caused by a bad battery, a short on a power rail, or the PMU itself.
steps: Fit a known-good battery.
Measure current draw with a DC power supply; look for abnormal draw or shorted rails.
Check the PMU and its rails; reball or replace if needed.

rules.title: Charging / USB IC problem
rules.why: The panic mentions the USB/charging controller (Tristar / Hydra / HPM).
steps: Try a known-good charging port flex and a genuine cable.
Inspect the charging connector for liquid damage.
Check or replace the Tristar / Hydra IC.

rules.title: Battery problem
rules.why: The panic mentions the battery or fuel gauge.
steps: Fit a known-good battery.
Inspect and diode-test the battery connector.

rules.title: Taptic engine problem
rules.why: The panic mentions the Taptic engine (vibration motor).
steps: Disconnect the Taptic engine and test.
Fit a known-good Taptic engine and check its connector.

rules.title: Audio IC problem
rules.why: The panic mentions the audio codec or audio amplifier.
steps: Disconnect the loudspeaker, earpiece and charging flex and test.
Check the audio codec and amplifier circuits.

rules.title: GPU / CPU problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the graphics part of the CPU.
steps: Restore iOS.
If it continues, suspect the CPU or RAM solder joints (board-level).

rules.title: Hardware watchdog reset
rules.why: The CPU stopped responding completely and the hardware watchdog reset it. This is usually board-level: power rails, CPU, or RAM.
steps: Check whether the phone also restarts in DFU / recovery mode (if yes, it is hardware).
Measure current draw and look for unstable rails.
Check CPU, PMU and (on stacked boards) the interposer.

rules.title: Always-On Processor (AOP) panic
rules.why: The Always-On Processor manages sensors such as the accelerometer, gyro and proximity sensor. A panic here often follows a missing or faulty sensor.
steps: Check the 'Missing sensor(s)' line if present.
Disconnect the front sensor flex and test.
Restore iOS if no hardware is found.

rules.title: Kernel data abort (software or memory)
rules.why: A kernel data abort is a crash inside iOS. On its own it is usually software. If it repeats with different addresses after a clean restore, suspect RAM / CPU solder joints.
steps: Update iOS, or back up and restore the phone.
If it keeps panicking after a clean restore, compare several panic logs: a different crashing process each time points to RAM/CPU.
Board-level: check CPU / RAM solder joints (reball).

rules.title: Memory exhausted (software)
rules.why: iOS ran out of memory. This is almost always a software or app problem.
steps: Update iOS and remove recently installed apps or profiles.
Back up and restore the phone.

rules.title: File system (APFS) problem
rules.why: The panic comes from the file system. This can be file-system corruption (software) or a failing NAND.
steps: Restore iOS.
If the restore fails or the panic returns, suspect the NAND.
